newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN IPOs - 1996 worst year for Indian firms.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN IPOs - 1996 worst year for Indian firms.

text.p: India's top primary markets' monitor said on Tuesday that 1996 was probably the worst year for the country's private sector vis-a-vis the primary capital market.

According to Prithvi Haldea of PRIME, the country's leading data base on the primary capital market, bad market conditions prevailing throughout the year forced medium and large-sized companies to shelve or defer their issue-raising plans.
While 80 percent of the total funds raised in 1994 were by the manufacturing sector, this fell down to 70 percent in 1995 and to a low 45 percent in 1996, PRIME said.

This resulted in an equity crunch and as such, according to PRIME, had a direct bearing on the industrial growth as is evidenced by the aggregate cost of projects financed through public issues which fell from 349,190 million rupees in 1995 to a meagre 90,050 million rupees in 1996, it said.
PRIME said the year was dominated by the finance sector.

As many as 418 issues (35 percent) and totalling 62,280 million rupees in the year were from this sector, garnering 55 percent of the total amount. In 1995, 451 companies had been from this sector who had taken up a much lower 30 percent share of that year's amount.

While public firms and financial institutions dominated the debt market (which included issues from IDBI, IRFC, Krishna Bhagya, ICICI, SCICI, IFCI, Maharashtra Krishna and Konkan Railway), the private sector too joined the bandwagon with offerings from Kotak Mahindra, TISCO, L&T, Arvind Mills, Mafatlal Finance and Gujarat Lease Financing.
PRIME's findings show that financial institutions and banks, in fact, assumed a dominant role in fund mobilisation.

Their share in 1995 was only 24,350 million rupees (raised by ICICI and IDBI) which worked out to 17 percent of that year's total amount. However, in 1996 the amount raised by FIs/banks jumped to 45,800 million rupees or 41 percent of the year's amount with almost all the FIs joining the fray including IDBI, IRFC, ICICI, SCICI and IFCI along with the twow bank issues.

PRIME said in a new development, the year saw the beginning of issues being offered through the bookbuilding route, though all the four issues so offered were for debt-ICICI, TISCO, L&T and Arvind Mills.

According to PRIME, calendar year 1996 finally closed with 1186 public issues mobilising a sum of 112,310 million rupees, net of firm reservations. Compared to the previous year, this represents an 18 percent decline in the number of issues and a 22 percent decrease in amount.

1996 would have ended on a gloomier note but for the first quarter of 1996 (January-March) which accounted for 503 or 42 percent of the year's issues. The market, which had already started deteriorating then, went into a steep fall and the balance nine months witnessed only 58 percent of the year's issues.

According to Haldea, the high number of issues in 1996 has been accounted for mainly by poor quality of paper including hundreds of finance companies or so called 'technical' issues. SEBI's effort to prevent finance companies from flooding the market failed miserably as 35 percent of the issues in 1996 came from this sector.

Significantly, issues from listed companies continued to decline from 93 in 1994 to 91 in 1995 and down to 57 in 1996, surely an indicator of the poor market conditions. Little wonder, 1129 of the 1186 issues (95 percent) in 1996 were IPOs, PRIME said.

Small issues continued to flood the market. As many as 627 issues (53 percent) were below 30 million rupees each. On the other hand, the year witnessed a total of 15 - 1,000 million rupees plus mega issues (17 in 1995). Of these, however, as many as 12 were debt issues compared to only one in the previous year, PRIME said.

The 1,000 million rupees plus debt issues in 1996 were from ICICI (10,000 million rupees), IFCI (8,000 million rupees), IRFC (7,500 million rupees), TISCO (5,000 million rupees), L&T (5,000 million rupees), IDBI (5,000 million rupees), SCICI (5,000 million rupees), Maharashtra Krishna (2,500 million rupees), Krishna Bhagya (2,500 million rupees), Konkan Railway (1,500 million rupees), Kotak Mahindra (1,000 million rupees) and Arvind Mills (1,000 million rupees). All of these evoked a good response from the public. The other instrument mega issues were from Bank of Baroda (8,500 million rupees), Dena Bank (1,800 million rupees) and Lloyds Finance (1,770 million rupees).

According to Haldea, the MS Shoes issue in early 1995 was the turning point for premium equity issues. All 1,000 million rupees plus issues which had opened prior to MS Shoes in 1995 had evoked a good response, these being from Reliance Capital (3,510 million rupees), Suashish Diamonds (1,020 million rupees), Jindal Photo (1,530 million rupees), Essar Oil (16,400 million rupes), Jindal Vijaynagar Steel (8,150 million rupees), Hindustan Petroleum (4,610 million rupees), Thermax (1,160 million rupees) and Binani Zinc (1,720 million rupees).

However, PRIME said, most such mega issues in 1995 which opened after the MS Shoes failed to enthuse the investors-these being from IDBI (19,350 million rupees), ICICI (5,000 million rupees), Mcleod Russel (2,700 million rupees), Pal-Peugeot (2,250 million rupese), Tamil Nadu Newsprint (2,200 million rupees), Malvika Steel (2,080 million rupees), Bhushan Steel (1,170 million rupees) and Pittie Cement (1,130 million rupees).
The 3,500 million rupees issue of MS Shoes, of course, was cancelled.
